Caribbean Stud Poker Basics: Ante, Raise, and the House Edge

Published October 2, 2026 · 8 min read · By the OddsLighthouse Editorial Team

Caribbean Stud looks like a lot like five-card stud poker at a glance — same hand rankings, same five cards each — but it isn't poker against the other players at the table at all. It's a single, fixed wager against the dealer's hand, with one raise decision that happens before you've seen a single card the dealer is holding. That one decision is where almost all of the strategy lives, and getting it right is the difference between playing close to the table's real house edge and giving away far more than the game actually requires.

How a hand of Caribbean Stud is dealt

Every player at the table places an ante before any cards come out. The dealer then deals five cards to each player, face down, and five cards to themselves, with one dealer card turned face up so the table can see it. Players look at their own five cards — there's no draw, no discard, no exchanging a card for a new one. What you're dealt is the hand you're stuck with for the rest of the round. From there, each player makes exactly one decision: fold and forfeit the ante, or raise by placing a second bet equal to twice the ante.

The ante and raise decision

Because there's no draw and no second look at your cards, the entire game turns on one choice made with partial information — your own five cards plus a single dealer up-card. Raise, and both your ante and your raise are in play, riding on how your hand compares to the dealer's once everything is revealed. Fold, and you walk away having lost only the ante, with the raise bet never placed at all. There is no in-between and no way to see more of the dealer's hand before deciding, which is what makes the decision rule below worth memorizing rather than guessing at the table.

Worth remembering: folding doesn't cost anything beyond the ante you already placed — the raise bet only exists if you choose to make it, so a disciplined fold on a weak hand caps your loss at a single unit rather than three.

Dealer qualifying: what happens when the dealer doesn't have ace-king

After every player has folded or raised, the dealer reveals their remaining four cards. For the dealer's hand to "qualify," it needs to be ace-king or better — any hand with at least an ace and a king as the top two cards, or any pair or stronger. If the dealer doesn't qualify, every player left in the hand automatically wins on their ante, typically paid at even money, while the raise bet pushes — it's returned with no win or loss, regardless of what the player was holding. This is a core part of the math: a non-qualifying dealer hand caps the table's winnings for that round, since the raise bet can't collect even if the player's five cards would have beaten the dealer's. If the dealer does qualify, every raised hand is compared against the dealer's hand individually, and antes and raises are paid or collected according to whether the player's hand beats the dealer's qualifying hand.

Correct strategy: the ace-king-or-better rule

Basic strategy for Caribbean Stud is a single, memorable rule: raise with ace-king or better, fold everything else — with one refinement. If your hand is exactly ace-king with no pair, check the dealer's up-card: raise unless the dealer's face-up card matches one of your unpaired cards below ace-king (your hand is ace-king-queen-jack-ten or weaker and the dealer shows a card that would have improved your hand had you held it), in which case the math shifts slightly toward folding. In practice, most strategy charts simplify this to "raise on ace-king or better, fold everything worse," which gets you extremely close to optimal play with far less to memorize than most table games built around partial information.

A worked example

Say a player is dealt ace, king, 9, 6, 2 — unsuited, no pair. That's exactly ace-king, the strategy threshold, so the player raises. The dealer turns over queen, jack, 8, 5, 3 with an ace showing on top — a qualifying hand (ace-king-or-better by virtue of the ace and the structure of the comparison), but it doesn't beat the player's ace-king-9. The ante pays even money, the raise pays according to the pay table for a hand that beats the dealer with no made hand beyond high cards, and the round settles in the player's favor.

Compare that to a player dealt king, 10, 7, 4, 2 off-suit — below the ace-king threshold. Correct strategy folds immediately, losing only the ante and never placing the raise, regardless of what the dealer eventually reveals. That single disciplined decision is what keeps an unplayable hand from compounding into a three-unit loss instead of a one-unit loss.

Pay table and house edge

HandTypical raise payout
Royal flush100 to 1
Straight flush50 to 1
Four of a kind20 to 1
Full house7 to 1
Flush5 to 1
Straight4 to 1
Three of a kind3 to 1
Two pair2 to 1
One pair or less1 to 1

Played with correct ace-king-or-better strategy, Caribbean Stud carries a house edge of roughly 5.2%, calculated against the ante. That's meaningfully higher than Three Card Poker or Let It Ride, both of which give the player more decision points and more information before committing additional money. Caribbean Stud's single blind raise, made before any dealer information beyond one up-card, is exactly why its edge runs higher — the player is taking on more uncertainty per bet than games that unfold in stages. As with any pay-table game, exact numbers shift by casino, and the mid-tier payouts (flush, straight, three of a kind) are where properties most often trim a point or two off the player's return.

The progressive jackpot side bet

Most Caribbean Stud tables offer an optional $1 progressive jackpot side bet, placed separately from the ante before the hand starts. It typically pays a fixed, escalating amount for a flush or better, with the full progressive jackpot reserved for a royal flush, and sometimes a smaller bonus for any flush regardless of the main hand's outcome. Like most progressive side bets across the casino floor — the same category covered in our blackjack side bets guide — its house edge runs considerably higher than the base game's, often into double digits depending on how large the jackpot has grown and how long it's been since it last hit. It isn't a free addition to a bet you were already making; it's a separate, generally worse wager that happens to offer a shot at a life-changing number.

Common mistakes

The most common mistake is raising on a hand below ace-king because folding feels passive — a king-high hand with a decent kicker still loses the raise bet more often than it wins once the dealer's hand is actually revealed, and the strategy threshold exists precisely because of that math. A second mistake is misunderstanding the dealer-qualifying rule and assuming a non-qualifying dealer hand means a bigger win; it actually caps the round, since the raise simply pushes rather than paying out. A third is treating the progressive side bet as a small, low-stakes add-on without accounting for how much higher its edge runs than the main game's. And a fourth is playing Caribbean Stud expecting it to behave like a draw-poker game — there's no second look at your cards and no way to improve a weak hand, which makes the single ace-king decision carry more weight than it might first appear to.

Frequently asked questions

Is Caribbean Stud played against other players at the table?

No. Every player's hand is compared only against the dealer's hand, independently. What another player holds or does has no effect on your own payout.

What happens to my raise bet if the dealer doesn't qualify?

It pushes — you get the raise bet back with no win or loss. Only the ante is paid out (typically even money) when the dealer fails to qualify with ace-king or better.

Can I draw or discard any cards in Caribbean Stud?

No. There's no draw phase. You play the five cards you're dealt exactly as they come, which is why the ante/raise decision carries so much of the game's strategy.

Is the progressive jackpot side bet worth playing?

It comes down to personal risk preference. Its house edge is generally well above the base game's, but it offers a shot at a large, sometimes life-changing jackpot for a small, separate wager — the same tradeoff found in most progressive side bets across the casino floor.
